facts.text: The study compared the as-printed alloy with a directly aged state produced at 750°C for 50 h.
Aging produced approximately 25–30 vol% homogeneously distributed Ni/Ti-enriched L12 nanoscale precipitates.
Aging also produced larger Al/Ti-enriched, Cr/Fe-depleted L21 precipitates located mainly near the cellular walls.
Both alloy states underwent isothermal oxidation at 600, 750, 900, 1050, and 1200°C for exposures of up to 96 h.
The oxidation specimens were polished coupons measuring 7.5 × 7.5 × 3 mm.
Oxidation developed a scale containing a continuous Cr-rich layer, primarily Cr2O3, between outer mixed oxides and an inner discontinuous Al/Ti-rich oxide region.
Preferential outward Cr diffusion formed a dense Cr2O3 barrier that restricted inward oxygen and outward metal-ion transport.
In the aged alloy, Cr-depleted precipitates delayed formation of a Cr-rich scale as protective as that formed on the as-printed alloy.
Additional precipitate–matrix interfaces in the aged alloy provided possible short-circuit paths for oxygen diffusion.
The aged alloy consistently exhibited greater oxidation mass gain than the as-printed alloy, and the difference became more pronounced as temperature increased.
The fitted mass-gain exponents at 600, 750, and 900°C were 0.59, 0.33, and 0.26 for the as-printed alloy and 0.64, 0.26, and 0.59 for the aged alloy, respectively.
The oxide-growth activation energies were similar: 154.07 kJ/mol for the as-printed alloy and 152.83 kJ/mol for the aged alloy.
